title: Scalable Hybrid Device Architecture on Thin-Film Lithium Tantalate for Long Distance Quantum Network Nodes with Atomic Frequency Comb Quantum Memories
abstract: Scalable photonic circuits are essential for realizing practical quantum networks beyond proof-of-principle demonstrations. Although diamond-based integrated photonics has been extensively investigated over the past two decades for quantum networking applications, its integration into scalable photonic platforms remains challenging. Quantum memories based on rare-earth-ion atomic frequency combs (AFCs) offer an attractive alternative; however, most demonstrations to date have relied on bulk free-space crystals, limiting their scalability for practical implementations. In this work, we systematically investigate the potential for hybrid integration of AFC-based quantum memories with a scalable integrated photonic platform. We propose a device architecture combining thin-film lithium tantalate (TFLT) nanophotonic circuits with ytterbium-doped yttrium orthosilicate (Yb:YSO) crystals for long-distance quantum communication. Our analysis shows that the hybrid TFLT-YSO platform offers a promising and scalable pathway toward integrated quantum memories and, ultimately, large-scale quantum networks.
summary: This paper proposes a scalable hybrid device architecture for quantum network nodes by integrating rare-earth-ion atomic frequency comb quantum memories into thin-film lithium tantalate (TFLT) photonic circuits. By selecting TFLT, the authors overcome scalability challenges associated with other materials, presenting a viable pathway for building large-scale quantum communication infrastructure.
main_problem: The primary challenge is realizing practical, scalable quantum networks by integrating quantum memories with robust, chip-scale photonic circuits.
main_result: The authors propose a promising and scalable hybrid architecture using thin-film lithium tantalate (TFLT) nanophotonic circuits coupled with ytterbium-doped yttrium orthosilicate (Yb:YSO) crystals.
method: The work involves a systematic investigation and comparison of various material platforms (e.g., TFLT vs. TFLN) to determine the best combination for hybrid integration, supported by rate and fidelity calculations.
model_or_system: The system is a hybrid quantum node combining a low-loss photonic circuit (optical routing layer) made of TFLT with a rare-earth-doped crystal (quantum memory layer) containing $	ext{Yb}^{3+}$ ions.
key_observables: Forward readout efficiency ($\approx 19\%$), spin coherence times (up to seconds), and calculated quantum network rates and fidelities.
important_parameters: TFLT's superior DC-bias stability under cryogenic conditions, and the ability to achieve low-loss coupling between the chip and the memory crystal.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling the quantum network link using specific parameters for source statistics (e.g., two-mode-squeezed-vacuum) and assumed efficiencies for components like the Bell-state measurement.
figures_summary: The notes reference tables comparing material properties (Table I) and comparing material platforms (Table II), and a final table (TABLE IV) detailing parameters for rate and fidelity calculations in the quantum network link.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by identifying the need for scalable quantum networks, reviewing limitations of existing platforms (diamond, bulk crystals), proposing the hybrid TFLT-YSO architecture, detailing the material selection process (favoring TFLT over TFLN), and finally quantifying the system performance using detailed rate and fidelity calculations.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering bottleneck in quantum networking by proposing a specific, manufacturable material stack (TFLT/YSO) to integrate quantum memories, which is crucial for advancing quantum information processing beyond lab demonstrations.
